title: Shaped Like a Swimming Goldfish: Suo-Oshima and Its Emigrant Villages
standfirst: Suo-Oshima's mountainous, sea-girt shape gave its people little farmland but centuries of seafaring skill. When Hawaii's plantations needed labor in 1885, nearly a third of Japan's first contract emigrants sailed from this one district. Remittances, a 1976 bridge and today's citrus orchards all trace back to that departure. This dossier follows the ground they left.

paragraphs.text: Suo-Oshima lies at the eastern edge of Yamaguchi Prefecture, a sea-girt territory rather than a single island. A district history published in 1923 describes its shape as resembling a swimming goldfish, broad in the southwest and narrowing toward the northeast, made up of the main island of Yashiro and more than thirty smaller islands scattered around it, and gives its size as seven ri and thirty-one cho (about 31 km) from east to west and six ri and twenty-two cho (about 26 km) north to south, an area of just over fourteen square ri. A 1928 prefectural guide puts the same district's coastline, following every inlet, at some twenty-eight ri, or around 110 km, in all. Ehime Prefecture lies across the water to the east and south, and the hills of Hiroshima Prefecture are visible to the north, across Itsukushima and other islands; the mainland districts of Kuga and Kumage face the district across a narrow strait to the west. The 1923 history counts many mountains and little flat land, with three ranges radiating from the central peak, Mount Kano; what plains exist follow the short Yashiro River, which crosses the middle of Yashiro village on its way to the sea, and the even shorter Miyazaki River at Kuka.

The 1923 history also repeats an old local claim: that the district was once its own province, Oshima-no-kuni, one of the 'great eight islands' of Japan's founding myths, before it was folded into Suo Province and survived only as a district name. Whatever its mythic status, the district was real enough to the powerful families, the Kono, Noshima, Kurushima, Murakami and Kuwahara among them, who held sway there through the late Muromachi period. Their independence ended in 1555, when Mori Motonari attacked the rival lord Sue Harukata at nearby Itsukushima; after that, the same history records, the island lords came under Mori command and the district became Mori territory.

The Mori domain governed the district through a local sub-administration, or saihan, created in 1651 with its seat at Kuka; the arrangement was briefly abolished and restored again within a few years in the early eighteenth century, but Kuka remained the district's administrative center for the next two centuries.

Elsewhere on the island, roughly contemporary private initiative reshaped the coast on a smaller scale. A domain retainer named Awaya Tatewaki, granted the tidal shoals off Komatsu in the 1680s, spent seven years damming the tide to lay out salt fields there, then a further six years building a harbor and a marketplace; a memorial inscription recorded in the district's own 1935 local-history compendium credits this work with founding the reclaimed 'Kaisaku' quarter of Komatsu that is still on the map today. It was this kind of small-scale land-making, salt pans, harbor works and reclaimed fields, that supported a slowly growing population before the nineteenth century opened a very different outlet overseas.

The old order ended, abruptly, in July 1866 (the sixth month by the old calendar), during the Second Choshu Expedition. Shogunate and allied forces occupied Kuka and Ageno-sho; a prefectural guidebook published two generations later still remembered Kuka as a place 'washed in fire and blood' by the fighting. Takasugi Shinsaku boarded the Choshu warship Heiin-maru for a night raid on the shogunate fleet on the 13th day of that month (24 July); two days later Choshu troops landed on the island and, after several days of fighting, drove the occupiers back to their ships. With Kuka burned, the district's administrative seat moved to Yashiro village, where it remained until 1896.

One casualty of the same campaign became, briefly, a figure of national history: Sera Shuzo, born in the district's Mukuno village in 1835, took up arms to help repel the 1866 attack on Oshima, then served the new imperial government as a staff officer during the Boshin War. Sent north in 1868 as part of the effort to pacify the Aizu domain, he was captured and killed by Sendai and Fukushima domain soldiers at the age of 32; his death is remembered today as the spark that pushed the northern domains into their alliance against the government he served.

sections.heading: The mountains that could not feed everyone

paragraphs.text: Meiji administration confirmed what geography had already decided. Yashiro's turn as district seat ended in 1896, when the office returned to Kuka; by 1920, the district's own statistical yearbook counted 81,643 people across its towns and villages. Citrus growing, which today occupies much of the island's slopes, was already under way by then: the modern town's own account traces cultivation's beginnings to the late Edo period. But the mountainous terrain the 1923 history described left little room for fields to begin with, and a growing population on a hilly, sea-locked group of islands had, by the late nineteenth century, few local ways to make a better living.

The 1920 population figures hint at how unevenly the district's towns had grown: Ageno-sho, with its sheltered harbor, counted over 11,000 people, more than either Kuka or Yashiro. Heigun, a separate island community of about 4,000 reachable only by boat, was different again: a 1928 guidebook describes most of its people as descended from the Mori domain's old ship crews. It was from villages across this whole district, not only Kuka and Yashiro, that the movement overseas would draw its numbers.

The opening came from abroad. In 1885, after Japan and the Kingdom of Hawaii agreed on a program of contract labor for the islands' sugar plantations, the ship City of Tokio carried the first 944 emigrants into Honolulu on 8 February. About three in ten of them, by the count the Japan-Hawaii Emigration Museum now gives, came from this one district. Over the following nine years of government-contract emigration, to 1894, some 3,913 people left Suo-Oshima for Hawaii, about 13.5 percent of the entire national total of roughly 29,000 contract emigrants, an extraordinary share for a single rural district of one prefecture.

The human cost showed quickly. A travel account of Hawaii published in 1889, only four years after the first ship, includes a necrology of Japanese who had already died there, among them people from several of the district's villages, Yashiro included. By the early 1920s the district's own records show its people no longer traveling only to Hawaii: its statistical yearbook lists departures and returns to and from the US mainland, Canada, Peru, Brazil, the Philippines, Mexico, Australia, Singapore and Java, evidence of a diaspora that had, within two generations, spread far beyond the sugar plantations where it began.

By 1928 the effect on the district was plain enough to print in a prefectural guidebook: many of the district's residents, it reported, worked abroad, and the whole district earned more than three million yen a year from it, so that all the islanders lived comfortably. One emigrant's story survives in brick and timber: Fukumoto Chouemon, born in Yashiro village in 1881, left alone for the United States at sixteen, made his fortune in trade, and returned to Suo-Oshima in 1924. Four years later he built a substantial house mixing Japanese and Western styles, at a cost the museum that now occupies it puts at some 30,000 yen, a considerable sum at the time.

That house still stands in Nishi-Yashiro, at the center of this dossier's district. In 2022 it was added to the national register of tangible cultural properties, and since 1999 it has held the Japan-Hawaii Emigration Museum, opened on 8 February, the anniversary of the City of Tokio's arrival. Among its exhibits is material related to King Kalakaua of Hawaii's 1881 visit to Japan, part of the diplomatic background to the emigration program that began four years later.

Ties to Hawaii outlasted the emigration itself. In June 1963 the head of the Oshima district's association of town mayors traveled to Kauai and signed a sister-island agreement with the county there, formalizing a relationship rooted in the district's own history of emigration to Hawaii. Exchange visits followed: high-school students went to a Kauai summer school from 1964, and in 1985 four Oshima town mayors and assembly chairs traveled to Hawaii for the centennial of the government-contract emigration itself, an anniversary marked two years later by a monument unveiled at Kauai's newly opened Lihue airport. The relationship's own fiftieth anniversary was marked by a ceremony at Kauai's county offices in October 2013.

In 1976, thirteen years into that relationship, the island's isolation from the mainland ended for good: the Oshima Bridge, a 1,020-meter span engineered with an unusual multi-column foundation to resist the strait's fast tidal currents, opened on 4 July, fulfilling what a prefectural tourism account calls a wish old enough to have been sung about in folk songs, and what a fiftieth-anniversary newspaper retrospective still described as a bridge that carried the islanders' happiness.

The island's local government caught up with these changes in 2004, when Kuka, Oshima, Towa and Tachibana, the four towns that had divided the old district between them, merged into a single Suo-Oshima Town. Citrus growing, which the town's own account traces to the late Edo period, has continued on the island's hillsides ever since, a slower, steadier transformation of the same mountainous ground that once pushed so many of its people overseas.

At the center of this district's study area, in Nishi-Yashiro, the Fukumoto house that Chouemon built with his American earnings still stands, its museum rooms arranged around the life he and thousands of his neighbors made abroad. The short Yashiro River, named in the 1923 district history as the area's largest stream, still runs down from the island's interior past Yashiro village to the sea nearby, much as it did when the first emigrants left. On the hillsides around it, citrus orchards, a much younger planting than the district's old rice and dry fields but grown here since the late Edo period, climb the slopes that the 1923 source described as leaving little room for fields.

From the shore near the museum, the view north across the water toward Hiroshima Prefecture is close to what the 1923 district history describes from this side of the island. The Oshima Bridge, a short drive west of Nishi-Yashiro, is worth the detour: before it opened in 1976, this strait was the only way on or off the island, and from its pedestrian walkway the fast tidal currents that shaped that isolation are still visible, racing beneath the deck.

timeline.what: Mori Motonari's victory over Sue Harukata at Itsukushima brings the island's powerful families under Mori control.
The Mori domain creates the Oshima saihan sub-administration, seated at Kuka.

Shogunate and allied forces occupy Kuka and Ageno-sho during the Second Choshu Expedition; after Takasugi Shinsaku's raid aboard the Heiin-maru on 24 July (the 13th day of the sixth month by the old calendar), Choshu forces retake the island from 26 July.
After Kuka is burned, the district's administrative seat moves to Yashiro village; a county office is formally established there in 1879, then moved to Kuka in 1896.
Sera Shuzo, born in the district's Mukuno village, is killed in the Boshin War at age 32.
The ship City of Tokio carries the first 944 government-contract emigrants to Honolulu; about three in ten are from Oshima District.
Some 3,913 people leave Suo-Oshima for Hawaii under the government-contract emigration program.
The district's population reaches 81,643; official figures also record departures to the US mainland, Canada, Peru, Brazil, the Philippines and beyond.
Fukumoto Chouemon, returned from the United States, builds the house in Nishi-Yashiro that later becomes the emigration museum.
Suo-Oshima and Hawaii's Kauai formalize a sister-island relationship.
The Oshima Bridge opens, ending the island's dependence on ferries to the mainland.
The Japan-Hawaii Emigration Museum opens in the former Fukumoto residence, on the anniversary of the City of Tokio's arrival.
Kuka, Oshima, Towa and Tachibana towns merge to form Suo-Oshima Town.

caveats: Kuka, the district's historic administrative and commercial hub and the site of most of the 1866 battle's surviving landmarks, lies several kilometers from the Nishi-Yashiro study center of this dossier; it is discussed here as district-wide context, and the walk below is kept to points verified at or very near the study center.

The 1923 district history's identification of Oshima District with 'Oshima-no-kuni,' one of the mythic 'great eight islands' of Japan's founding stories, is that source's own traditional claim rather than a settled scholarly identification, and is reported here as such.
Emigration totals differ slightly between sources; this dossier follows the Japan-Hawaii Emigration Museum's own published figures (944 on the first ship, 3,913 from Suo-Oshima in 1885-94).

A 1920 statistical table of yearly departures and returns by destination country could be read for its list of countries but not reliably for exact yearly counts, since OCR could not confirm the alignment of columns and rows; this dossier therefore reports only the population totals and the list of destinations from that source.

The individual named in Suo-Oshima's own 2013 newsletter as having signed the 1963 Kauai agreement is not repeated here by name, since this dossier could not independently verify the correct romanization of his personal name from the source alone.
